newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: INTERVIEW-Venezuela's Poletto upbeat on CVG sale.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Venezuela's Poletto upbeat on CVG sale.

text.p: The long-awaited $3 billion sale of the steel and aluminum companies of Venezuelan state holding company Corporacion Venezolana de Guayana (CVG) has a good chance of going ahead this year, a government minister said.
"I'm more optimistic than pessimistic, but there are risks," Venezuelan Investment Fund (FIV) president Alberto Poletto, with portfolio for privatization, told Reuters in an exclusive interview.
"I believe there is a possibility of failure, but success is more likely," said Poletto, adding that the sales are scheduled to take place before the end of the year.
With the financial, environmental and legal audits now completed, and sales contracts agreed upon both by potential buyers as well as the Cabinet, the next step is Congressional approval.
Poletto said the sales contracts would go to Congress within the next two months.
"In general, the major political parties are aware of the importance of the privatization," he said.
"But we'll do all the lobbying we have to, and be as flexible as we can ... I hope Congress gives it their full urgency".
The sale is seen by many analysts as high-profile test of Venezuela's economic reform spirit and an end to the country's former model of state-led economic development.
But years of mismanagement have left the loss-making companies riddled with corruption and special interests that have slowed progress in readying them for sale.
Analysts say that if the sales are not closed by early next year, at the latest, they will be postponed until after presidential elections in December 1998.
"We've been hard hit by special interests both inside the CVG as well as outside ... privatization would end all that, that's one of our objectives," Poletto said.

With the buyers set to assume environmental clean-up costs at the aluminum companies estimated at $250 million, Poletto added that following the sale "that money could go towards education and health instead."
However, the bauxite concession for the aluminum smelter Venalum and Alcasa still has to be finalized, as does the port concession at Puerto Ordaz on the Orinoco River.
"But these are bureaucratic fine touches, little more," said Poletto.
The persistently niggling point of a Japanese consortium's refusal to give up a 20 percent veto share in Venalum before the sale will also be left for the investor to settle, Poletto said.
"Venezuela has reached a fundamental agreement with the Japanese, the investors will do the last part," said Poletto.
The Japanese group includes Showa Denko KK, Kobe Steel Ltd, Sumitomo Chemical Co Ltd, Mitsubishi Materials Corp, Mitsubishi Aluminum Co Ltd and Marubeni Corp.
Thirteen companies have qualified to bid for the aluminum sector, including Alcoa, Gencor, Alumax, Reynolds Metals Co, Norsk Hydro ASA and RTZ Corp.

Eleven companies have qualified for steel company Sidor's sale, including Mexico's Hylsamex SA, Imexsa, and Ahmsa ; Brazil's Usiminas, and Companhia Siderugica Macional ; Japan's Kobe Steel, Argentina's Rand Siderar SAIC and Venezuela's Sivensa.
((-- John Paul Rathbone, Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
